Kuṟuntokai 130. Veḷḷi Vīti(yār): the confidante / SHE

lg.l: taṉṉayan teḷittalun talaippiri vaccamu
miṉṉiyal vaṉpoṟai yeytuta larumaiyu
muyireṉak kūṟalu māṟṟiṉaṉ peyartaluñ
ceyirtapu kātaṟ ṟeyvap puṇarcci.
[The hero] making clear his desire; [the hero’s] fear of separation;

[the hero’s] encouragement of [the one with a] sweet nature;Does iṉ iyal vaṉpoṟai refer to the hero’s sweet-natured encouragement, or the encouragement of either the sweet-natured one (i.e., the heroine) or the heroine’s sweet nature? Based on the poems cited in the commentary, I lean towards the second or third option, which are practically very similar. For a fuller discussion on the meaning and function of the term vaṉpoṟai, see the translation notes to the koḷu to poem four of this cūttiram. [the hero’s] difficulty obtaining [her];
[the hero] saying, ‘[She is like my] life’; and [the hero feeling] comforted then departing
– [these are] the divine union of faultless love.

div.p: eṉpatu collap paṭṭa pākiṉ uṭ ṭeyvap puṇarcci yām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which the divine union occurs within the aforementioned division.

muṟ cey viṉai kāraṇam ākak kaṇṇuṟṟup puṇarnta piṉpu talaimakaṉayappuṇarttalun teruṭṭalum pirivaccamum vaṉpoṟaiyum eytutal arumaiyum uyir eṉṟalum āṟṟip peyartalum eṉap paṭṭaṉa teyvap puṇarcci yām eṉṟa vāṟu.

lg.l: koṅkutēr vāḻkkai yañciṟait tumpi
kāmañ ceppātu kaṇṭatu moḻimō
payiliyatu keḻīiya naṭpiṉ mayiliyaṟ
ceṟiyeyiṟ ṟarivai kūntali
ṉaṟiyavu muḷavōnī yaṟiyum pūvē.
Pretty-winged bee whose life is examining honey,
without saying [what I] want, tell me what you saw!
Are those flowers you know also fragrant
like the hair of the young woman with close-set teeth

the nature of a peacock, of a love united [and] well-practised?payiliyatu keḻīiya naṭpiṉ is not clear. In this interpretation, it refers to a love that endures over multiple births. Within the context of this cūttiram, whose topic is a love fated to occur because it had existed in previous births, this makes sense and is supported by the commentary.

div.p: eṉpatu nayappuṇarttiyatu.
This is [the hero] having expressed [his] desire [to the heroine].

lg.l: yāyu ñāyu mārā kiyarō
ventaiyu nuntaiyu memmuṟaik kēḷir
yāṉu nīyu mevvaḻi yaṟituñ
cempulap peynnīr pōla
vaṉpuṭai neñcan tāṅkalan taṉavē.
My mother and your mother, what are they [to each other]?
And my father and your father, what of their relationship?Alternatively: ‘how are they related?’
And I and you, how shall we know [each other]?
Like the falling rain and the red earth,
[our] loving hearts have mixed together.More literally: ‘loving hearts have themselves become mixed’.

div.p: eṉpatu teḷittal.

This is [the hero] making clear [his desire].This is not obvious to me, but I understand that this is when the hero, understanding that his life and the heroine’s life are now inextricably linked, says something to that effect to comfort and please her. This is also the sense communicated in the IAC quote provided as a source for the koḷu.

lg.l: iṉaiyal vāḻi pirivoṉ ṟilaṉē
naṉaimalar naṟumpūṅ kōtai
yamaiyē ṉiṉṉaiyā ṉakaṉṟa nāṉṟē.

Don’t despair! Live on! I am without any separation.The idea is that the hero has no intention of leaving her whatsoever. Another way to translate and understand this would be: ‘I am without a single [thought of] separation.’
O [one with] a flower garland fragrant with blossoming buds,

I will not be contentamai-tal is polysemous, and I see multiple sensible ways of understanding it here. The presented translation follows the general idea found in the cited sources, that the hero will not be able to bear separation, although amaiyēṉ (‘I will not be satisfied’) expresses this in slightly weaker terms than āṟṟēṉ (‘I will be unable to bear it’), found in PK 10.3, to the best of my knowledge. The other interpretation I entertained was to take amai-tal as ‘to befit’, in which case the hero would not befit their relationship if he left. on the day that I depart from you.

div.p: eṉpatu pirivaccam.
This is [the hero’s] fear of separation.

lg.l: āṟṟiṉaṉ maṉṉō neñcē piriyiṉ
āṟṟā ḷivaḷeṉa vaḻuṅkiṉa māka
vāṟṟā nilaimai kaiviṭ
ṭāṟṟā ḷāyiṉa ḷāyiḻai yataṟkē.

I truly did indeed endure, O heart.The nuance of the particle -maṉṉō is not immediately obvious. It normally carries the weight of an assertion posed as a question: ‘Surely…?’ Here, I am inclined to take this as a combination of an assertion and a lament, conveying the hero’s sense of frustration and helplessness at the situation. As we suffered, thinking,aḻuṅkiṉam can be understood as: ‘as we desisted [from separating]’. The translation presented makes more sense in light of the final line. It provides the heroine with a more concrete cause for her pain – the hero’s suffering – than him not leaving, which is what she was initially worried about. In addition, it more closely resembles the IAC passage it is based upon (see source layer of the apparatus), where the heroine mirrors the emotions of the hero. In this case, he suffers so she suffers.
‘If we separate, she will not be able to bear it’,

having done away with her [initial] disconsolateāṟṟā nilaimai kaiviṭṭu in line three is more literally: ‘having relinquished the state of not being able to bear [the separation]’. In practice, this refers to a state of mental weakness and despondency. state,
the girl with the choice jewels [now] cannot bear that.āṟṟāḷ āyiṉaḷ āy iḻai yataṟkē is literally: ‘the one with the choice jewels has become one who cannot bear with regard to that (our suffering)’.

div.p: eṉpatu vaṉpoṟai.

This is the encouragement.What does vaṉpoṟai mean here? Following the sequence laid out in the IAC, we expect the hero to provide assurance and comfort to the heroine. In the context of the next poem, to which this koḷu also applies, this fits perfectly. However, in other ilakkaṇam treatises, this situation is normally expressed by vaṉpuṟai. This is what we find in the corresponding section of the IAC, cited in the apparatus. Is there a difference in meaning and application of vaṉpuṟai and vaṉpoṟai? Looking to the kiḷavi-s – the other place where these terms appear – it seems as though there is none. Both terms nearly always appear as part of a set phrase: (word for heroine) vaṉpuṟai/vaṉpoṟai etir-tal (‘the heroine, in the face of encouragement…’; see NA 31, NA 38 for vaṉpuṟai; see KT 319, NA 218 for vaṉpoṟai). Here I follow this evidence, and take vaṉpoṟai as ‘encouragement/assurance’. This just about encapsulates this poem, which reads primarily as the hero’s response to his own efforts to appease the heroine. Takahashi notes that in a later stage of the relationship, when the hero goes off to war after their marriage, vaṉpuṟai is the term for the confidante’s encouragement of the heroine, and vaṉpoṟai is used for the heroine’s acceptance of that encouragement (Takahashi 1995, 211). If we transpose that onto this situation, then the two poems treat the heroine’s reception of the hero’s encouragement, which only fits the first poem cleanly.

lg.l: iṉaiyal vāḻi yemmūr malarnta
paḻaṉat tāmaraik keḻīiya vaṇṭuniṉ
kaṇṇeṉa malarnta kāmar cuṉaimalar
naṇṇi nāḷu nalaṉuka rummē.
Don’t despair! Live on! The bee, which united
with the lotus blooming in the water tank in our village,
will approach the lovely mountain-pool flowers

that blossom like [your] eyes, and daily enjoy [their] goodness.nalam is a broad term in akam poetry, encompassing the heroine’s beauty, desirability, and a more abstract feminine excellence. Some translate it as ‘virtue’, but this carries a moralising connotation that is absent from the older poetry, where nalam is something perceived and enjoyed rather than upheld. Here, the bee’s enjoyment of the flowers’ nalam mirrors the hero’s enjoyment of the heroine’s. I translate it literally as ‘goodness’ to preserve this breadth.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: maṉavē ralkuṉ maṭantai kūṭṭam
kaṉavē teriyiṉ yāvatu
naṉavē yeṉiṉu naṇṇalō varitē.
Union with the girl whose hips are beautiful with chank beads –

[it is] a dream, when examined.teriyiṉ can be understood differently. Here it is taken as ‘to enquire, investigate’. The other possible interpretation would be to take it as ‘to be understood’. In this case, the phrase would translate to: ‘If it was understood that the union with the girl… then even if someone…’. Even if it were at all real,
approaching [her would] stillThe particle -ō is used to convey a sense of lamentation. be so difficult.

div.p: eṉpatu eytutal arumai.
This is [the hero’s] difficulty obtaining [the heroine].

lg.l: pulaṉaṉ ṟeṉpa viṉṉuyi ratuvē
yalarmulai yākan tāṅki
nilavoḷi matiyi ṉilavume ṉuyirē.
They say it cannot be perceived, [this] sweet life.

[And yet,] carryingThe absolutive tāṅki should share the subject of the finite verb, giving eṉ uyir as its subject: ‘my life, bearing a chest of budding breasts, shines…’. One could, however, take the heroine as the implicit subject of tāṅki and read eṉ uyir as the subject of nilavu alone: ‘[She,] bearing a chest of budding breasts – my life shines like the moon, bright with moonlight’. This would arguably better reflect the source poems (PK 20, PK 21), where the hero sees his uyir in the heroine’s visible form rather than attributing her form to it. If tāṅku-tal could be read intransitively here – ‘my life, borne by a chest of budding breasts’ – that would provide the sense closest to the PK poems, but I find no evidence for such a usage in the corpus. a chest of budding breasts,
my life shines like the moon, bright with moonlight.

div.p: eṉpatu uyir eṉak kūṟal.
This is [the hero] declaring, ‘[She is like my] life’.

lg.l: kaṉavē yāyiṉu naṉavē yāyiṉu
nalviṉai tantatoṉ ṟaṉṟē yataṉāṉ
melliya lāka mēvavum peṟumē.
Whether in a dream or in reality,

is this not something brought by good actions?I take the particle -ē here as an interrogative, in practice marking a rhetorical question appended to the negative root al – something like, ‘isn’t it so?’. Taking it as an emphatic would give the opposite sense to the poem, which would make no sense contextually. aṉṟē could otherwise be understood as ‘on that day’, which would make sense in the context of the hero appreciating the role of his past actions in bringing him to this point. The line would translate to: ‘This is something good actions/karma brought that day.’ Were this to be the case, one would expect aṉṟē, as the temporal locus, to precede the verb.

By that, I will be united againEither this indicates that their initial union had already occurred, or that they had been united in past lives. In general, this poem and the koḷu are clearly based around the idea that their relationship is karmically ordained.
with the breast of the one with a soft nature.This could just as well be: ‘united with [her] soft-natured breast.’

div.p: eṉpatu teyvan tuṇai yākak koṇṭāṟṟip peyarntatu.

This is [the hero] having left after understanding that [the heroine] is his divine[ly ordained] companionI have understood tuṇai in its oldest meaning, ‘companion’, but this would also make sense taking it as ‘support’. In that case, the hero would leave, feeling comforted that he had divine support in uniting with the heroine again. In terms of the general sense of the koḷu, there is little difference between the two translations. and feeling comforted.

lg.l: uṭaiyai vāḻi neñcē yiṭaikoṇ
ṭaḻuṅka lōmpumati taḻaṅkoli mikunīr
vaḻuttūr kākkum puṇaiyiṉ
viḻuttuṇai cāṉṟa mikuperuṅ kiḷaiyē.
Live on, O heart!

Understand [this]I understand iṭai koṇṭu as ‘having taken in’ (i.e., having understood). Another option would be to understand the phrase adverbially, in which case it might refer to being ‘in the middle of [trouble]’, for example in the roaring waters at Vaḻuttūr. Though this emphasises the comparison between the hero’s friend and the raft, it stretches the meaning of koṇṭu. Alternatively, one could take the phrase literally: ‘grab the middle (of the metaphorical raft), and protect [yourself] from suffering!’ puṇai is postpositioned to iṭai, so one would have to deviate from standard syntax to an unreasonable extent to justify this interpretation. and protect [yourself]In Caṅkam literature, ōmpu-tal is nearly always found in the imperative and in those cases it generally means ‘beware’, so a warning. In this case, that does not make very good sense. A slight semantic shift took place in the epics and bhakti, broadening the scope of the root from a sense of protection to encompass ideas of removal. My impression is that this better describes its nuance in this poem. from suffering!

Like the raft that protects VaḻuttūrIn line with UVC and others who have written about the possible authorship of this text, I have treated Vaḻuttūr as a proper name, possibly of the village where the text was composed. It is the only reference to a place in the TNV and it appears once more in this text, in TNV 17, poem 35. It could, however, be an epithet, in which case it simply means ‘a praiseworthy village’.
from the water that swells with roaring sound,

you possess a very great friend,Contextually, one has to understand kiḷai as ‘friend’. There is no indication that his companion is any blood relation, and it cannot be referring to any kind of group here, as the referent of kiḷai is then described as a companion. worthy of [being considered] an excellent companion.The oldest attested meaning of tuṇai is ‘companion’. In this context, I think it carries the clear nuance of ‘help’ or ‘support’, a later semantic shift (cf. AiN 325.4; Kuṟaḷ 36.2, 41.2, and many more). I think it justifiable to speak of a certain expectation of aid from a companion, so I keep the older sense.

div.p: eṉpatu pāṅkaṉai niṉaintāṟṟip peyarntatu. 15.
This is [the hero] having left after thinking of his friend and feeling comforted.

Cf. AV32: teyvan taṉiṉe ytavuṅ kiḻattiyi | ṉeytavum paṭūu miyaṟkaip puṇarcci ||

UVC’s correction here makes sense. It was included in the errata to the first edition. These were nearly all incorporated into the second edition, but this one was not. I believe this was a simple oversight. The same correction was implemented in the koḷu to the second example poem. Theoretically, one can make sense of both readings. teḷital is intransitive, in which case the hero’s desire would become clear to the heroine through his elliptical address or actions. Reading teḷittal suggests that the hero actively makes clear his desire. There are no obvious parallels I am aware of in this exact context, but the evidence from the commentary gives a clue. It glosses this word with teruṭṭal, which is transitive and means ‘to make clear’. There are no variants for that reading, and so this edition follows that evidence and prints teḷittal.

This cūttiram follows the same sequence as the IAC, but the corresponding passages are included as sources for the commentary. This is because the wording is more similar in the commentary and, in previous cases, the commentary has very clearly been closely based on the IAC, whereas the cūttiram has not.

A note on the terminology for this union: the later term teyvap puṇarcci, found in this text, suggests a more moralistic, ‘karmic’ initial meeting – the union in this life has been fated due to two lovers’ relationship in their past lives. As for kāmap puṇarcci, the term found in the oldest grammars, the precise connotation is not clear. Nakkīrar understands it as a union out of their increased desire when they meet alone (IAC 2), in which case kāma carries a clear sexual undertone. Takahashi, however, argues convincingly that in the earliest strata of Tamil literature, kāma was a broader term better translated as ‘love’ (Takahashi 1995, 66–67). The two other terms used for this meeting, at least according to Nakkīrar (IAC 2), are also quite ambiguous. muṉṉuṟu puṇarcci refers to some union that has been experienced before and is understood to refer elliptically to this initial union. The most common term for this – iyaṟkaip puṇarcci – could also mean a number of things. The union may be ‘natural’ either as they chance upon each other (where their other meetings need to be organised through intermediaries), or because it has been divinely ordained. According to Nakkīrar, whom later scholars largely follow on this point, these four terms all refer to the exact same thing (IAC 2, p. 47).

vāṭkai is noted as a western dialectal variant by the Tamil Lexicon and perhaps vāṭkkai is a variant of that. No citations are provided. Thus, due to the lack of textual evidence and for ease of comprehension, the standard spelling is chosen.

Could this be another example of C1 representing a as ai? Otherwise, one has to read the nonsensical aim ciṟait tumpi (‘five-winged bee’). This reading is not reported in Wilden (2010). As this is not a known variant anywhere else, and since it makes no sense, the standard canonical text is printed.

Cf. IAC2, p. 54–55: niṉaintu, aṟintēṉ, taṉṉaiyāṉ kātaṉmikaviṉāṟ pārāṭṭappōlumeṉa uṇarntu yāṉ taṉṉai muṉṉiṉṟu pārāṭṭa ivvakai melivuceṉṟa perunāṇuṭaiyāḷ puṟattu oruvar ivvoḻukkattai uṇarvār kollōveṉṟu uṭkoṇṭa ñāṉṟu ivaḷ iṟantupaṭumpōlumeṉap periyatōr āṟṟāt taṉmaiyaṉāyiṉāṉ.
Cf. PK10.3–4 (IAC2, p. 56): niṉṉiṟ piriyēṉ piriyiṉu māṟṟē ṉeṭumpaṇaittōṭ | poṉṉiṟ pacuntoḷi vāṭaveṉ ṉāṅkol pulampuvatē ||
Cf. PK11.3–4 (IAC2, p. 56): peyvaḷait tōḷiniṉ ṉiṟpiriyēṉ | maṇiniṟam poṉṉiṟa mākaveṉ ṉāvi varuntuvatē ||
Cf. PK12.3–4 (IAC2, p. 56): muciṟi | yaṉṉāy piriyēṉ piriyiṉu māṟṟē ṉaḻuṅkaṟkavē ||

The Tamil Lexicon cites the Tivviya Pirapantam for this seemingly alternative spelling (“nāṉṟu”) of the more well-attested ñāṉṟu. Since this is the reading of C1 and it is attested elsewhere, it is chosen. It is a valid alternative spelling. It seems as though the other readings are corrections (in the case of C2, an incorrect attempted correction) or standardisations.
Cf. IAC2, p. 56–57: aṅṅaṉam āṟṟiṉāḷatu nīrmaiyaikkaṇṭu ivaḷ evviṭattum ekkālattun taṉṟaṉmai eṉpatu oṉṟu ivaḷ, eṉṟaṉmaiyaḷē pōlumeṉap periyatōr kaḻiyuvakai mītūr niṉṟu vaṉpuṟaiyeṉpatōr coṟcollum.
Cf. PK14.2–4 (IAC2, p. 57): toṇṭi yaṉṉāy tuyaralemmūr | maṇiniṟa māṭattu māṭṭiya vāṉcuṭar mālainummū | raṇiniṟa māḷikai mēṟpakal pārit taṇavarumē ||
Cf. IAC2, p. 57: aṅṅaṉaṅ kēṭṭa talaimakaḷ emperumāṉ aṇittemiṭameṉkiṉṟāṉāl, aṇiyataṟku arumaiyillai eṉkiṉṟāṉām
Cf. AV129.4: itamaṇit teṉṟal

It is impossible to know in which variety of āciriyappā this poem was composed. Of the 174 anonymous poems in the TNV, 163 are in the nēricai variety, where the penultimate line has three cīr-s, and the remaining eleven poems are composed in nilaimaṇṭila āciriyappā, where all lines have four cīr-s. C1 transmits three cīr-s in the penultimate line, and KKms transmits four. The meaning of the poem hardly changes with or without this cīr. As the collection is predominantly nēricai āciriyappā, I think it more likely that a cīr was lost somewhere along the line of transmission, bringing the poem in line with the majority, than one was added.

The IAC has been cited as it mirrors the basic syntax of the TNV poem and has the same basic idea – their villages are close together and so he will be able to visit her easily and regularly. This is expressed in the prose passage quoted, where the heroine realises what the hero is saying and feels comforted.
The AV closely mirrors the language found in the IAC prose passage quoted.
Cf. PK17.3–4 (IAC2, p. 59): meṉ ṟōḷitaṉ ṉākam puṇarntatellāṅ | kaṉavē naṉavāy vaṭiṉumey tātiṉik kaṇṇuṟavē ||
Cf. PK18.3–4 (IAC2, p. 59): peṇṇaṇaṅkiṉ | ṟirunalañ cērntatel lāṅkaṉa vēyeṉṟu cintippaṉē ||
Cf. PK19.3–4 (IAC2, p. 59): maiyēr taṭaṅkaṇ maṭantaimel lākam puṇarntatellām | poyyē miṉimeymmai yāyiṉu millaip puṇartiṟamē ||
Cf. TK17.4: puṇarppō kaṉavō piṟitō vaṟiyeṉ

There is a clear strand of transmission that is only broken by either a scribal error or emendation by UVC when he made the paper copy of the palm-leaf manuscript. He read “kaṉavu” (‘dream’) with the most common interrogative particle -ō. However, every other reading of this poem takes the particle -ē, which can also be an interrogative particle, at least according to TC 258n. This edition takes the more well-attested reading for this reason. In addition, it keeps the sort-of-rhyme in the first cīr of each line – not ubiquitous in this collection of poetry, but nevertheless preferable when it occurs.

Cf. PK20 (IAC2, p. 60): tēyat tavaruyi raippula ṉaṉṟeṉpar cennilattaik | kāyak kaṉaṉṟetirn tārmaru mattuk kaṭuṅkaṇaikaḷ | pāyac cilaitoṭṭa pañcavaṉ vañcippaim pūmpoḻilvā | yāyat tiṭaiyitu vōtiri kiṉṟateṉ ṉāruyirē ||

Cf. PK21 (IAC2, p. 60): iṉṉuyir kaṇṭaṟi vārillai yeṉpa rikaṉmalaintār | maṉṉuyir vāṉceṉ ṟaṭaiyak kaṭaiyaluḷ veṉṟuvaiyan | taṉṉuyir pōṉiṉṟu tāṅkumeṅ kōṉkollit tāḻpoḻilvā | yeṉṉuyi rāyat tiṭaiyitu vōniṉ ṟiyaṅkuvatē ||
Because the exact same phrase – pulaṉ aṉṟu – is found in PK 20.1 (provided on the next page as a source), upon which this poem is most likely based, this edition reads the same.
Cf. IAC2, p. 60: āḵtu yātōveṉiṉ tāṉeytiya āraṇaṅkākiya avvuruviṉai niṉaintu tāṉeytum upāyamāvatu taṉkātaṟ ṟōḻaṉai itu koṇṭu muṭikkuṅ kollōveṉpatu.
One would not expect to find gemination after an imperative form.
vaḻuttāl, found in C1, would be a conditional, which would not make sense here. vaḻuttūr is also referenced in another poem in this text (TNV 17, poem 35) and is read by the KK.
Cf. IAC2, p. 49: nayappeṉpatu talaimakaṉ vaṇṭiṟku uraippāṉāyt talaimakaḷ kēṭpat taṉ nayappuṇarttiyatu.
Cf. IAC2, p. 55: pirivaccameṉpatu, tāṉ pirivu añciṟṟum pirivaccam; avaḷaip pirivu añcuvittatum pirivaccam; ātaliṟ pirivaccameṉappaṭum.
Cf. IAC2, p. 57: vaṉpuṟaiyeṉpatu vaṟpuṟuttuvatu.
Cf. IAC2, p. 59: kāṭṭiṉāḷaik kaṇṭu, ivaḷai yāṉ eytiṉēṉeṉak karutiṉaṉ! eytiyatuṇṭēṟ kaṉāpōlum! naṉavē yāyiṉum ivaḷ eṉakku eytutaṟku ariyaḷāmeṉa āṟṟāṉāyiṉāṉ.
Cf. IAC2, p. 60: atu paṟṟukkōṭāka āṟṟi nīṅkumeṉpatu.
Cf. AV128: aiyan tīrttal pirivaṟi vaṟuttaleṉ | ṟeytiya vaṉpuṟai yiruvakaittākum ||

There seems to be some confusion amongst scribes between the common vaṉpuṟai and vaṉpoṟai that we find in the TNV. Rajarethinam records vaṉpoṟai as a variant for vaṉpuṟai in his edition of the AV. I am inclined to understand this as a simple orthographic variation, possibly a regional one, and so I have retained this uncommon form.

The TNV begins its enumeration after the ‘prologue’ – four situations that precede the first union. The TP indirectly mentions them, the IA does not, and the IAC mentions them explicitly, as does the AV. They are: kāṭci, aiyam, tuṇivu, and kuṟippaṟital.
